sections.content: This course is extremely helpful since this is a project building a real system from scratch! Throughout the project work, I gained practical experiences that are beyond theoretical learning, particularly with respect to system design, implementation and debugging. I included this experience too in my CV since it is a highly relevant skill that showcases my proficiency in working with complex projects.
sections.teaching: Percy & Chris are very courteous and helpful. When any question arises or clarification is required, they are always there to answer and the overall learning experience is a lot easier and less stressful. They gave us some great guidance all through the class.
sections.grading: Concentrating and paying attention on accidental errors is required since the exams were quite easy so careless mistakes would make a huge difference on grading.
sections.workload: This is as the project must do a lot of coding that needs to be completed in time. Consequently, a long time is logged on bugs that are fixed frequently, sometimes a lot. Working in a group can be more challenging when you are dealing with some very diverse working habits and working timetables (with bad code scattered evenly across different components). We really need to understand that the group project experience relies heavily on group dynamics. This can be extremely detrimental if the group is made up of freeriders, because each individual member’s contribution needs to be at the heart of the wider achievement. The good news is that I had some relatively loyal group members that were responsible for most things and willing to work. But when a good team had members all working at uneven speeds there were still bumps. One often had to rush before deadlines for something with deadlines. Due to the scale of work, I strongly suggest taking my project from a baseline. To meet the immediate pressing time limit, planning ahead and distributing task distribution early can reduce the pressure later on. Also consider leaving some days before the deadline to tackle unintended bugs or integrations that sometimes won’t come back to haunt your effort on a project the size of this one. Overall, this course is a lot rewarding despite the huge amount of work and offers meaningful experience that I think would be extremely valuable for future projects and continued professional growth.

sections.content:

Can refer to the comment earlier from other user for the grading scheme. But I think the grade is good if you know the requirement. The previous user might get bad grade because of the project, coz you see the weight of project is high! so pay attention to the things I say in the workload box about the projects. Then your hardwork will be rewarded.

btw exam are non-cumulative. pretty stright forward just need to be careful with careless mistakes
sections.workload:
1 lecture + 1 lab per week. The lab is long but insightful

The project is the biggest workload as you had to work with another 6 ppl. I don't know anyone so I form group with 6 random ppl. 1 girl is soo hardworking and the rest are so-so. 2 near freerider who abusely use AI.  Me and another girl carry the whole project, but I think the workload is manageable. I do the whole code for user-side within 3 day. If you took Isom 3400 before it will be a huge advantage. Also the lab will provide enough sample code for you to use. And AI is allowed as long as you can explain the code. So it is not that hard. You just has to think from the user perspective and be user friendly, adjust the UI and design. And try to input any random thing and click any button in random order, just think the user is stupid and try to break the system. And your task is to do input validation and fight with this stupid user to avoid them breaking the system. That's it. I spend most of the time enhancing the user input validation and UI. For UI side, try to make things as user friendly as you can with your common sense. Eg your code should remember the member ID once they login, but not manually ask them to type again when they need to change their personal info. Just make the system easy to use like a corporate one, follow your common sense.

Pay attention in lab, TA told us what they want, what part to pay attention to (eg things i said before). Just follow them and meet the requirement then you are fine.

Finally we got pretty nice comment from the TA and of course high marks in project. Full marks in demo.

(FYI, i am final year with credit overload this sem, but I really don't think the workload is that high as rated by other ppl. Maybe I got 1-2 good groupmate to work with and i myself enjoy coding. AI helps a lot when you need debugs.)

sections.content:
The course content is rich, practical, and useful in the industry. Objectively, the content can earn an A for this course.

Lecture contents:
1. Entity Relationship Diagram (ERD)
2. Enhanced Entity Relationship Diagram (EERD)
3. Transformation
4. Normalization
Some practice examples are explained on lectures after those for theories.

Lab contents:
1. Drawing ERDs with Data Modeler
2. SQL statement -- Data Definition Language (DDL)
3. SQL statement -- Data Manipulation Language (DML)
4. User Interface (UI) construction in Python
sections.teaching:
Objectively, for this part I should give a B. The teaching is quite good overall. Concepts and rationale are clearly explained and there seems to be more exercises provided compared to previous semesters.

Percy was quite professional, and he was passionate in his lectures. He pushed us to answer his questions and do excercise from time to time, but only after a lecture could you realize how unbelievably efficient he was.

Chris and Samuel replied to questions very promptly. Their labs are meticulous and rich in content. You can expect to learn a lot from them. My suggestion is, don't hesitate to raise questions and schedule consultations with them, especially when it comes to your group project.
sections.grading:
Project differentiates people, and the grading for this part is arbitrary (Note that this course is essentially a "DESIGN" course! You can't associate mark deduction with mistakes precisely, like what you can do for exams. It's totally about the raters' opinions). My comment for this part was supposed to be an F, but sadly I didn't have the choice.

The grading scheme is as follows:
Lab submissions (10%): Attend all labs and submit a proof of your presence. The tasks for the first half of labs are usually harder, but for the second half that should be fine.

My performance: The mark is not counted directly to the final result and the result is not disclosed, so I can only roughly describe my performance.
First half: 2.5/5
Second half: 5/5

Midterm (24%): The percentages of exams are the realized ones. The nominal ones separate a 4% quiz from midterm, but actually they are integrated.

My performance: 17.7/24 (mean+0.21sd)
After scaling, of 24 marks we have
Mean: 16.95 (70.6%)
Max: 21.7 (90.4%)
Min: 5.5 (22.9%)
SD: 3.49 (14.54%)
Median: 17.85 (74.4%)

Final (31%): The percentages of exams are the realized ones. The nominal ones separate a 6% quiz from final, but actually they are integrated.

My performance: mean+0.88sd

Project: Three blocks for this part. My team's project as a whole was rated mean-1.53sd, which was totally inhuman and nonsense -- so long as you are a normal learner (i.e. attend all labs, collaborate with teammates, put in average time and effort) you can score higher than this sh*t, let alone a group like mine, who have worked hard throughout the semester.

Oftentimes, the rater(s) would grab on a small detail that was not user-friendly enough and deduct substantial marks from you. But such mistakes do not affect the usage of the basic function, just making it not so convenient. For example, after searching for the "basic information" about a course, if you want to look for the "detailed information" of that course, and your system cannot automatically copy the course ID to the "detailed information" block and require manual input of ID instead, than you are busted. The worse thing is, since I cannot check out other groups' projects, the rater(s) can tell whatever he/they believe is right. I clearly have no idea how they rate other works, so I have no choice but to take that grade. Appealling to this part is basically useless.

Progress demonstration (5%): Demonstrate the preliminary version of your database via an online meeting. Scheduled at the end of October.

My performance: half mark (very low among the groups)

Database system demonstration (20%): Demonstrate the final version of your database via an online meeting. Scheduled at the end of November.

My performance: Not disclosed

Project report (10%): A report of your group project. It should be no longer than 20 pages.

My performance: Not disclosed

Final grade: C (Rank: 58/73)
Just look at the grade distribution on USThing. At this moment it's 21% A range, yet 33% for C range and below. The rater can really go to the HELL for this s**t.

It's quite normal to think that the similar tragedy won't happen on you (I hope not. Whoever wants to take this course, bless you.), and the guy who's writing this comment is probably a s*cker. But to be very honest, as a final year student, I have never got a C-range grade other than this throughout my whole university life. I should have told you more about me, but think about this first: why bother getting around with this sh*t when you have better choices in other majors?
sections.workload:
The workload was insane. It's my final year in this university, and from my perspective, the only courses that have workload as large as this one are LABU, which are already dead. Therefore, the course definitely deserves an E in this part.

First you have a 2-hour lecture and a 3-hour lab each week. Though on average it's fine, but for such long time you are required to take in massive content and work out intensive excercises almost without any room for distraction. Luckily, for the lab you've got a 10-minute break. That made the labs more acceptable.

Then you have a midterm and a final. No surprise for that, since these are 4-credit course must-have.

The most horrible stuff was the group project. Forming a group of 7 was already hard in the first place. Then you got phased tasks every week. Soon as you arrived at November, you could barely stop working. My group's final version of database was built up with approximately 2500 lines of Python code. Apart from that, your group would be required to submit a report as well as an ERD. If you ever wanna take a break in the middle, make sure you have enough lifespan for staying up late during the final weeks.

sections.workload:
The workload should be lighter than the previous years since the tools used in the group project are only Oracle sqldeveloper, Oracle datamodeler and Google Colab now, though it's still heavy and depends on your groupmates' attitudes and abilities.  There are no more “software only available in G005” issues now, which means you can work on your project anywhere on your laptop with your groupmates (even remotely) as long as you have access to the aforementioned applications.  Expect to use Python for the project since ipywidgets’ taught during the lab for the interface creation.
Speaking as someone who had never touched on python again since ISOM2020, just ISOM2020/basic programming logic knowledge is enough to handle the course and complete the project in python.  
For the final exam, do not think you can just shit the project and that's the full extent of your loss, because the very same project python codes taught in labs will come back later to haunt you again in the finals if you don’t understand how they work. And I think you are good to go if you care to spare some time to find some more online exercises to do for your exam preparations (eg. SQL).

sections.content:
It is a practical and technical course. It required many of your own knowledge/ mindset to build a database and a purchase system. This  course  emphasizes  both  theories  and  hands-on  experience. It includes  a  group  project  in  which  students  design  and  implement a database system to solve a practical business problem. Oracle will be used as the main software package for students to gain hands-on experience.

Usage of software will be taught during lectures which is so useful so make sure you download it before class.
sections.teaching: James is a good professor as he was able to answer different kinds of question given some of them are too situational. Samuel is a fun tutor and he always try to interact with students though it is hard through zoom.

In COVID sem, two quiz was merged to one, and that one quiz was hard as hell. The time was inadequate and I only completed 6-70% of it. However, I still managed to get a B+ so I think project was counted heavily.
sections.workload: Although the syllabus was already cut. It was still HEAVY in workload. Especially before project demonstration. In our semester, the deadline was postponed since everyone request for more time to work on it. So avoid being a deadline fighter in this course otherwise you will only be able to present a half done system and get a bad grade!

sections.content:
Most technical IS course as it requires extensive SQL programming knowledge in order to build a database system for the project.

Note that SQL will be taught in lectures, however for the project, PL/SQL will need to be used. So make sure you learn both effectively.

For the project, you will need to use 3 software programs, Toad Data Modeler, SQLTools and Oracle Forms. Get familiarized with them asap as the can be confusing to use at the start.

Toad Data Modeler will be used mainly at the start of the semester to build the ER diagram.
Then you will need to use Oracle Forms to build the actual interface of the database and SQLTools for data validation, testing, debugging etc.

This course can be quite challenging at times if you're not a technical person so it is imperative that you put extra effort into it. Depending on your groupmates' preferences, you can work on the ER diagram, project reports and build the easier functions for the database. If you can get the help of people who are experienced in SQL, that will be very helpful as you can get your work done faster rather than spending ages trying to figure out what is wrong in your code.
sections.teaching:
As mentioned in other reviews, Muller is a great professor and he is very helpful.

I have sat even in James's classes and he is also pretty good. He tends to explain in a more conversational way and expects students to actually do the exercises beforehand as he will ask volunteers to do the exercises on the board. Whereas Muller would solve it in class one by one.

Samuel is a great TA and he explains very well. He has been teaching this course for years now so pay attention to the tips he'd give for the project.
sections.grading:
Project accounts a large percentage of the grade, so you need to work hard and contribute as much as possible. There will be 2 peer evaluations in the semester, the 2nd one will affect your final project score. Make sure you form a good group as you'll need to meet your teammates frequently throughout the semester.

The midterm and final are more or less straightforward, just do the assigned exercises thoroughly and understand the lecture content well and you'd be just fine.
sections.workload:
You'd probably know by now. The course is extremely heavy in workload. The reason being that the software that needs to be used for this project is only available in the lab computers. A few people managed to install the software on their personal computers/ laptops. Samuel will probably tell you the details about it in the lab, but this method can be very difficult as personal laptops don't have the processing power required to handle these software programs.

Expect to work on the project about 2-3 times a week assuming nobody in your group has any SQL background and towards the project demo, you could literally be coming everyday to the lab to work on it. I'd advise you do this course in a semester where you don't have other challenging courses or else your workload will be too much too handle. Otherwise if you can manage to do this course on your Exchange, please do so and avoid the pain that you'd potentially need to experience at UST.

Get started on the project once the ER diagram concepts have been taught as this will form the foundation for the rest of your project. There will be 2 project demonstrations in the semester, so as they draw closer, the labs would be full and hard to secure a good computer as some barely work. Plus the lab tends to stink quite bad cuz of the number of people inside and food :P

sections.content: This course covers the basic concepts and principles of database design and implementation. Database management systems that are the foundation of any information systems must effectively store and manage data with integrity and security. This course emphasizes both theories and hands-on experience. The course work includes a group project in which students design and implement a database system to solve a practical business problem. Oracle will be used as the main software package for students to gain hands-on experience.
sections.grading: Since everyone is scoring similarly in the midterm, project and final exam is far more important. The time you spent on your group project reflects your grade the most. Overall the grading is good if you have contributed enough in your project and revise the exam thoroughly.
sections.workload: The only thing you have to do is the group project, if you are paying attention to the labs and lectures, you will able to finish your project already.

sections.content:
Before Midterm:
- Entity-relationship model (a bit similar to class model in ISOM3210 but they are not the same things)
- Enhanced ER model

After Midterm:
- SQL: data definition language (DDL) and data manipulation language (DDM)
- Logical Database Design: transforming ER diagram into relations and Normalization
- Physical Database Design, Data and Database Administration: some theoretical knowlege of managing a database systems

This course teaches you how to design and implement a database system based on some business rules.
You will learn how to structure a database such that the data could be stored effectively with integrity (ER model). You will have a taste of drawing ER Model with Toad Data Modeler in a tutorial session.
You will also learn a programming language (SQL) that allows you to build a database with Oracle Forms, manipulate it and retrieve data from it.
I personally think this course is the most practical and all-rounded IS course of all.
sections.teaching:
Muller is the BEST professor I have ever met. He is so dedicated and reachable. He is able to explain every concept and logic in a clear manner with lots of examples. The exercise he provided is sufficient for exams preparation. If you are not confident with some topics (for me, it's writing SQL subqueries) you can also find Muller after class or in his office. He can understand your struggles and teach you in another way that you will eventually get it.

Samuel is a SUPER knowledgeable and friendly TA. He is an expert of programming. You should pay a lot of attention in his tutorials, though each session lasts for 3 hrs :( , as he speaks almost no bullshit. Everything he taught in the tutorials is gonna help you with your project. Try to test your program as much as you can, because he is so experienced that he can always spot bugs and tell you which part you can improve to make your systems more user-friendly.
sections.grading:
Practical Submissions 6%
Project 33%
Midterm Exam 26%
Final Exam 35%

The grade is proportional to your effort. Project means a loooooot to your grade and your understanding in the exams so don't ever try to, or even think of being a free-rider!!! The exams are straight forward. It should not be a problem, as long as you can do the exercise given by Muller and Samuel on your own.

**Tips for final: Be focus when you are transforming the ER diagram to relations and be careful of the answer format in the Normalization, or you may miss out some points. SQL is the BIG BOSS. Make sure you save enough time to do the last part of the paper.
sections.workload:
This course is infamous for its heavy workload. You are going to build a database system (tea shop point-of-sale system) from scratch with 6 groupmates. Only computers in G005 are equipped with SQL Tool and Oracle Forms, so you can only work on the project when the lab is available, usually on weekends, or you may try to sneak into the lab while people are having other lessons (if you are not kicked out). Our group divided the job evenly and we have no previous knowledge of SQL at the beginning (I suppose). None of us is free-rider, but still, we ended up staying at G005 every night and every weekend.

**tips 1: Start the project ASAP! After you have learned how to draw ER model, draw it for your project right away! Better to leave more time to the end to combine your works, test the final product and debug.
**tips 2: Sources from previous students might help a little. You can refer to their codes and user interface if necessary but it is not possible to copy their system entirely because no two systems are the same.
**tips 3: Separate the job evenly. Do not put all the burden on one groupmate who seems to be better at programming. Not only he/she is going to hate you and score you low in peer evaluation, it is very obvious when you cannot answer Samuel's questions in progress demonstration.

sections.content:
This is an introductory course to database design and administration and this is also one the required courses for the IS major.

The course content covers topics like entity-relationship diagrams, SQL (mostly data definition language and data manipulation language), transformation of relations, normalisation, data, and database administration.

The content is chosen appropriately for beginners to database design, and the topics build upon each other therefore it is important to understand each of the modules thoroughly so that you are not confused in the subsequent chapters. There is a recommended textbook, and while it is not necessary, I would recommend trying to obtain a copy of it as the book does give additional explanations on topics which may be useful to clarify any doubts you may have.
sections.teaching:
I would say that Muller (Prof. Cheung)'s teaching style is excellent. I really enjoyed all of his lectures, and I found that he presented all of the content extremely clearly and used examples were relevant to elaborate on any points and to illustrate the theories. He was also very to-the-point, such that he doesn't spend time talking about topics that aren't assessed. I would advise you to go to all of the lectures because they are extremely useful and can help you to consolidate your understanding. There are also exercises provided after every chapter so that you can test your own understanding of the topic, and these are very useful when preparing for the exams. Although the lectures are almost 2 hours (there's only one lecture a week), Muller does provide breaks in between so that you have some time to stretch your legs. That being said, don't sign up for the evening lecture if you're prone to feeling sleepy on a Friday evening. :)

I think most IS major students have had Samuel as a TA during their time at UST, so I won't spend too long commenting on the lab sections. The lab duration is 3 hours as indicated in the class schedule, however, Samuel only teaches for the first 1.5 hours and the remainder of the time is for you to work on your project (DO actually work on your project as this time is super valuable and you can also ask Samuel for any help with issues you may have). I will say that for implementing some of the project functionality, you may have to go beyond what is taught in lectures and the lab sessions.
sections.grading:
The course grading scheme includes:

— Lab Submissions (6%)
— Project (33%)
— Midterm Exam (26%)
— Final Exam (35%)

The grading is relatively fair, although the final project score was not released therefore I cannot comment on how this component is graded.

The midterm exam covers the first four chapters, and in this semester, the mean was around 80/100 with an SD of 8. The final exam is non-cumulative and focuses on the topics taught after the midterm. The mean for the final exam was around 69/100 with an SD of 11.

The grading for the project is a bit unclear, however, most groups receive pretty much the same score for the progress demonstration (as told by Samuel, the TA). I will say that the project can influence your grade significantly, so I would not recommend taking it lightly (I'll elaborate on this in the Workload section).
sections.workload:
This is a 4-credit course, and the majority of the workload comes from the project. Although the case may vary each semester, it typically involves building some sort of database system for a company and implementing various functions for the end user as specified in the project brief. The software for working on the project (mainly Oracle Forms Developer and SQLTools) is only available in G005, and as the demonstration deadlines approach, it's near impossible to find a free computer (so go early and claim a bunch of desktops if you want to be a deadline fighter). In addition, collaboration is also quite tough therefore you'll be doing a LOT of compiling of different versions in addition to all the debugging (debug very thoroughly, because you'll get caught out in the demonstration if you don't do this). I would also recommend finding groupmates who have strong coding skills as this may make it easier for you to do the SQL coding when building the forms, and a small mistake in the code can take you ages to figure out so be careful.

Aside from the project, there isn't a lot of additional workload. Although Muller provides exercises for each topic, he usually dedicates part of the lecture time to working on these and walking you through the answer, so you don't necessarily have to do them before class (unless you just really want to test your database knowledge immediately after the class).

sections.content:
This is an introductory course in SQL. If you study ICT - Database module in HKDSE, you can nearly skip most of the class.

What we learn in class is useful for lab and exam. Extra stuff learned during lab session will not be examined.

Useful for understanding in database management
sections.teaching:
Muller and Samuel are very good.

Muller's class is very useful because he won't waste time to say anything that is out of the course requirement. He always hit the main point and he will provide useful examples for us to follow. Even if you never learn SQL before, he is very patient and willing to answer your questions.

Samuel is a very nice TA. He is super helpful and will stay with us to help with our project even when it is out of lab session. You can always find him easily in LSK G005. HAHA~
sections.grading:
Fair grading. You need to work hard on both project and exams.

There are 2 easy assignments and mean is around  2.7/3. Assignments are similar to exam so remember not to copy from others but really do it to test your understanding.

Exams are similar to COMP course, you have to work on SQL to solve some requests. Midterm need to draw ERD, EERD and simple DDL, Final is non-cumulative. Final cover SQL(DML) and normalization(1NF,2NF,3NF). Both exams have MCs and short questions(or long).

Grading Scheme

Assignment(s)   6%
Project          33%
Midterm Exam   26%
Final Exam 35%

My score:

Assignment 2  3/3

Final Grade: B
sections.workload:
The workload is very heavy so please make sure you find your responsible friend (who has the programming background) to study this course with you.

6 people in a group and Samuel let us form our own group.

As we need specific software that is only available in LSK G005 (you can't find them in virtual barn) and it is uneasy to install all those software, you need to work in G005 all the time for your project. Before progress demo and final demo, some people will work in G005 until midnight (YES! midnight!)

Spare some time every day after class to work on the project might help.

reviews.instructor: CHEUNG, Yat MingTSE, Sheung Hei Chris

sections.content:
The content of this course can be divided into two main parts. One is technical part, such as ERD, Normalisation, SQL. One is just knowledge part, such as concepts of Data mining, Database Administration. For me, I think the diffcult part would be the technical part. Drawing disgram and Writing programming is actually quite hard for some students since business students are generally not good in this aspect. The concepts learnt in ISOM3210 and 3230 would definietly be helpful in dealing with this course. The course content is actually quite useful when you are dealing IT related jobs in futures. (Personally, I think it would be better to include more topics about open source database.)

SQL should spend the most time to learn. ERD and normalisation just be careful of the logic behind and some minor stuff.
sections.teaching: Muller and Chris taught the content is a quite good way. Although attendance is not required, they suggested it was good to attend and I did agree with them. It would be better to listen to what they said in lessons. There are something they would explicitly mention during lectures and tutorials. (You will know why it is so important when you are doing the project.) And they are really nice when it comes to answering your questions in project and exam content.
sections.grading:
Good Grade as ISOM3210, If I remember correctly, median is around B. So all you need to do is study two days before and find yourself a 'god' groupmate :)

sections.workload: Previously, the course has two mid terms and one finals. Now we only have one mid-terms and one finals. It would be quite easy for a 4 credits course. However, the most difficult would be doing a project. This semester we are instructed to construct an online sales system. WARNING: You are suggested to find at least one groupmate who is good at programming (JAVA, VBA, C++,etc.), otherwise you will be in a disaster typing code during any free time in weekend. And you can only test your code in G005/G012 only. Exams' MC part is not very difficult, but writing SQL is the most challenging part.
